bearings.paper_claim: Locality is neighbours not yet covered by the partial solution (Eq 3). Greedy reaches at least 99 percent of optimal on small graphs (Table 1b: BP-500 b=20 GCOMB 0.998, greedy 0.99, optimal 1). GCOMB matches greedy on real graphs and wins mainly on time at scale.
bearings.paper_location: Sec 3.3 Eq 3 p.5; Sec 4.2 Table 1b and Figs 2b-2e p.6-7
bearings.system_side: budgetRecruit is greedy max coverage. Gain = (1 - cov[c]) + sum over v of PE[c][v] times (1 - cov[v]), with cov = 1 - prod(1-p) over selected recruiters. Candidates below max(1, 0.1 x mean degree) are skipped. The budget in $k becomes a seed count via K.CEDGE. The live caller passes target -1, so the target multiplier is off.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The 1-1/e bound holds for cardinality-constrained monotone submodular coverage, which this objective is. Paper evidence for greedy near-optimality is only on 500 to 900 node graphs (Table 1b); applying it to a 533-member graph is an extrapolation. The GCOMB Eq 3 locality is a Q-learning state feature. The code uses the plain coverage marginal, which greedy already contains, so the GCOMB label overstates the mapping. The degree prune is a fixed rule, not the learned noise predictor.
bearings.verifier_note: Code confirmed as described: gain, cov update, 0.1 x mean degree prune, target -1 path, K.CEDGE conversion. Paper claim softened: Table 1b greedy/optimal ratios are 0.953/0.963 (BP-500 b=15, about 98.96 percent) and 0.93/0.941 (Gowalla-900 b=6, about 98.83 percent), so 'at least 99 percent' is the authors' rounding, not the table minimum. Eq 3 confirmed on p.5 as a Q-learning state feature. The 533-member size was not verified in this pass.

bearings.paper_claim: GCOMB's advantage is wall-clock speed on large graphs: about 10 times faster than greedy on MCP; speed-up over CELF on YT falls from 4.0 at b=20 to 2.01 at b=200 (Table 2b). Training saturates within 10 minutes (Fig 2a, synthetic BP 5k). Sequential and capacity-constrained problems are named as future work (Conclusion p.9).
bearings.paper_location: Sec 4.2 p.7 (Table 2b, Figs 2d-2e, Fig 2a); Conclusion p.9
bearings.system_side: Joint CU budget optimizer: heap-based lazy greedy over equal $500 chunks (INC) of a $2.5M pot (BUDGET), with a per-member cap PMAX of $10k. The queue is rebuilt after each conversion. Members behind the stance gate receive nothing. This is capacity-constrained allocation over about 533 members, not set selection on a large graph.
bearings.code_ref: fec/engine/optimize.py:27 (BUDGET, INC, PMAX definitions); fec/engine/optimize.py:126-151 (heap loop, queue rebuild, re-push)
bearings.transfer_conditions: The 10x and 2.01 to 4.0 speed-ups are for MCP on real graphs of 1M+ nodes, not for a small capacity-constrained allocation. A GCOMB-style learned policy would fit only pure set selection without per-member caps at much larger scale. The paper reports no quality gain over greedy.
bearings.verifier_note: Heap lazy greedy, INC 500, BUDGET 2.5M, PMAX 10k and queue rebuild on conversion all confirmed. optimize.py never names CELF; the module docstring calls it lazy greedy. Table 2b speed-ups (4.0 to 2.01) and 10x over greedy confirmed. The 10-minute saturation is Fig 2a on synthetic BP 5k, not a large-graph speed claim. Sec 5 limits GCOMB to set problems and names sequential and capacity-constrained problems as future work; 'explicitly excludes' overstates it.

bearings.paper_claim: IM is evaluated with single-colour Independent Cascade, with expected spread averaged over 10,000 Monte Carlo simulations. GCOMB spread is within small differences of IMM (Table 3a, largest magnitude about 3e-3 at YT-TV b=50) and 30 to 160 times faster.
bearings.paper_location: App A Def 4 (IC); Sec 4.3 p.8 (text and Table 3a)
bearings.system_side: budget_frontier.py runs a heap-based lazy greedy up to MAXSEEDS 60. Spread is a two-colour competitive cascade (pro versus anti seeds) at MC 20 with common random numbers. Knee = last seed whose marginal is at least a quarter of the peak marginal.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's 1-1/e and IC comparisons assume submodular single-cascade spread. The two-colour race with bystander mobilization need not be submodular, so those guarantees do not transfer. MC 20 has no convergence check by the paper's standard of 10,000 runs. The 30 to 160 times speed figure is versus IMM, not versus this frontier.
bearings.verifier_note: All code claims confirmed: MC default 20, MAXSEEDS 60, heap lazy greedy, cascade is a two-colour IC race with keyed draws, quarter-peak knee rule. Paper claims confirmed: 10,000 simulations (line 712), Table 3a largest entry about -3 x 10^-3 at YT-TV b=50, 30 to 160 times faster (line 715). Paper spread-difference units are unclear, as the ext notes. Verdict is reproduced for the bearing as written; the transfer caveats stand.
